newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy to Vietnam now appears in offing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy to Vietnam now appears in offing.

text.p: A spokesman for the Republican-led Senate Foreign Relations Committee said on Monday he expected no further hitches to confirmation of President Bill Clinton's choice to be the first U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

Committee Chairman Jesse Helms' spokesman predicted probable smooth sailing for the nominee, retiring Representative Pete Peterson, a Florida Democrat and onetime prisoner of war in Vietnam. "The constitutional impediment is out of the way so I don't see any reason why Mr. Peterson wouldn't be confirmed that we're aware of right now," spokesman Marc Thiessen said.

The Senate delayed acting on the nomination last year on the grounds it violated Article 1, Section 6, of the Constitution barring a Congress member from appointment to an office created, or for which the pay was changed, during his or her term.
With a new Congress convening on Tuesday, the White House plans to send Peterson's name to Capitol Hill again this month and no problems are anticipated, an administration official said.

Helms, a North Carolina Republican and archfoe of communism, opposed Clinton's July 1995 decision to establish diplomatic ties with Vietnam, but Thiessen said he will give Peterson "the normal consideration process that we would for any other nominee."

"If you had to send an ambassador to Vietnam, Mr. Peterson is probably one of the better ones at that," he added in a telephone interview. But he said Helms, who has criticised Hanoi for allegedly withholding information on Americans still listed as missing from the Vietnam War, was reserving his decision on Peterson until after the hearings.
The U.S. Embassy in Hanoi is currently headed by Desaix Anderson, a career foreign service officer with the title of charge d'affaires.

Sen. Craig Thomas, the Wyoming Republican who heads the Foreign Relations subcomittee on East Asian and Pacific affairs, plans to hold confirmation hearings for Peterson as his panel's "first order of business," probably early next month, his spokesman, Dan Kunsman, said.

If confirmed as expected, Peterson would become the first U.S. ambassador in Hanoi. Previous U.S. envoys were accredited to the U.S.-backed South Vietnamese government in Saigon that was overrun by the Communist-ruled North in 1975.
Peterson's plane was shot down in 1966 and he spent six and a half years as a prisoner of war. He retired from the Air Force as a full colonel in 1981.

Virginia Foote, director of the U.S.-Vietnam Trade Council, which groups companies doing business in Vietnam, said the long-delayed posting of a U.S. ambassador would be "very important" for broadening bilateral ties.

"This will indicate that the U.S. continues to move forward in the overall relationship with Vietnam," she said in a telephone interview. "All of economic normalisation needs to be done still," she added, referring to the possible future granting of most-favoured nation trade status, Export-Import Bank financing and the signing of a trade agreeement.

Diehard U.S. prisoner-of-war activists have said they still oppose sending an ambassador to Hanoi because Vietnam has not done enough to account for Americans known to have been alive in Vietnamese captivity but still unaccounted for.
"We're totally opposed to sending anybody as U.S. ambassador," said Ted Sampley, a long-time activist who is publisher of the U.S. Veteran Dispatch in Kinston, North Carolina.
